At least one of the subpoenas was delivered after a federal judge rejected the Justice Department’s effort to force California to immediately set aside 20,000 ballots from people it claims are “likely noncitizens.” Such voter fraud is exceedingly rare. The court determined the move would wreak havoc with an election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters, and discount the votes of citizens. The subpoenas order the election officials to testify before a grand jury in a criminal investigation on November 4, the day after the election. ... ## Famine Declared in Yemeni City of Taiz Amid Houthi Siege In Yemen, the governor of Taiz says the city of roughly 1 million people has entered into famine due to a weekslong siege by fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis. Human Rights Watch said Thursday the siege could amount to the war crime of using starvation as a method of warfare. The famine declaration came as a Saudi airstrike on Taiz killed 13 people. That followed a Houthi attack on Aden’s airport that injured passengers and halted flights.

items.title: New economic data challenges Fed chief’s not-too-hot perspective By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - New data may challenge Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s sense that the US economy can handle a robust expansion without stoking inflation, as a key measure of price pressures jumped and strong consumer spending and business investment pushed growth further beyond the level most central bank officials see as sustainable. ... The jump in third-quarter gross domestic product, announced on Thursday by the US Commerce Department, however, was even faster than anticipated, with output growing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the July-September period, consumer spending rising by a robust 3.8%, and investment in business equipment up a massive 20.9%. The pace may not continue. Consumer spending, for example, ... But the data in hand still show an economy that so far has not slowed despite the outlook for tighter monetary policy, with strong demand now coinciding with broad-based inflation. Different measures of inflation’s breadth show anywhere from roughly 50% to nearly 60% of the items in the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the gauge the Fed uses for its 2% inflation target, posting annual price increases of more than 3% in September — far above pre-COVID-19 norms for a measure Warsh said he sees as a good indicator of underlying inflation trends. Though the number of items above that 3% level fell slightly last month, Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said the details of the PCE report showed inflation was broadly persistent across the economy, particularly in service industries where Fed rate hikes may have less of an impact.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. ... There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.excerpt: Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said Friday that higher interest rates will be needed in the near future to rein in inflation. "I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon," Musalem said in prepared remarks for the Shadow Open Market Committee, a gathering of economists focused on the central bank. Musalem's comments offer the first morsels of insight into what leaders at the Fed see next following Wednesday's decision to hold interest rates steady. It will also bolster the view among investors that the Fed will return to hiking rates at its next meeting in December. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in a roughly 76% likelihood of the Fed lifting rates by a quarter percentage point at that gathering, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later," Musalem said. "Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth." ... But Musalem warned that inflation is "too high," citing the personal consumption expenditures price index released Thursday that showed annual inflation above 3%. Fed officials have been closely monitoring inflation expectations among consumers and investors to ensure they don't get too far above the central bank's long-term target of 2%. He said there's a likely scenario where inflation remains above 2% into the future unless the Fed adjusts monetary policy.

items.title: Fed’s Barkin says US central bank’s direction ’straightforward,’ the question is pace, SiriusXM reports By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Richmond Federal Reserve President Tom Barkin said on Friday that with high inflation and the economy solid, the path of US monetary policy was "straightforward," but with an open question about the pace of any future rate increases. "Inflation’s high, demand is solid, unemployment is relatively low. So I think the direction of travel is pretty straightforward," Barkin said on SiriusXM’s Business Briefing when asked if the Fed would need to raise rates again. "The question, though, is pace ... We signaled a gradual approach. Gradual makes sense when you’re not much behind the curve, where you want time to learn." At this point, however, Barkin said that businesses in his mid-Atlantic and southeastern district report both rising cost pressures and a willingness to pass those costs along, with booming investment in artificial intelligence boosting demand and an array of prices. "There are a lot of cost pressures that are hitting American businesses," from diesel fuel to computer chips or the wages for skilled labor, Barkin said. "In the context of four or five years of elevated inflation I think it is just easier to make the argument... We are going to have to" raise prices. "That lived experience of inflation does affect future inflation, unless of course the Fed does something about it."

items.title: Trump escalates legal challenges, scrambles schedule as US midterm elections near By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Oct 30, 2026, 06:11 AM Updated Oct 30, 2026, 12:36 PM ... By Andrew Goudsward and Jarrett Renshaw WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump stepped up legal efforts that could help his fellow Republicans challenge results in next week’s midterm congressional election, and scrambled his schedule for the campaign’s final days on Friday, restoring planned rallies he had scrapped a day earlier. Early voting outpaced 2022 totals, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail for the November 3 contest in which nonpartisan analysts believe Trump’s Republicans are likely to lose their current majority in the US House of Representatives, with control of the Senate expected to be hard fought. The Trump administration pushed forward in legal cases in Alaska, home to a Senate contest that may play a pivotal role in determining the majority, and California, which historically takes more time than most other states in counting ballots. The Justice Department filed an amended lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday seeking to block the certification of results in the event of a narrow Republican loss, citing a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler candidate with a nearly identical name to the Republican incumbent. In California, meanwhile, the Justice Department is escalating its pressure campaign against state election officials, issuing subpoenas as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters. Taken together, the moves are an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told ⁠Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington. The dispute in Alaska, home to one of about 10 highly competitive Senate races, could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority from Republicans. If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they could launch investigations into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran. TRUMP’S CANCELED RALLIES ARE BACK ON On Friday, Trump will campaign in Florida, hoping to galvanize his supporters in a state he won handily in 2024 but where early voting has tilted toward Democrats. It will be his latest stop in a state Republicans usually expect to win, following campaign events earlier this week in Mississippi and South Carolina. Less than 24 hours after canceling, the president plans to hold weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa after all, alongside "nearly 20" virtual campaign appearances before Tuesday, according to a White House official. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday. "The last year and a half, it’s been difficult," she told the crowd on Thursday at an event in Macon, Georgia. "Now we’re in the phase where we can do a whole lot." More than 46 million Americans had already voted early as of Friday morning, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, surpassing the total from the 2022 midterms. Among them was Chicago native Pope Leo, who became the first pontiff to vote in a US election, the Vatican press office announced on Friday, which follows Leo’s critiques of Trump’s war on Iran and treatment of immigrants as deviating from the teachings of Christ. ALASKA SENATE DISPUTE In its revised lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday, the Justice Department wrote that operatives for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola orchestrated a "sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters." The New York Times reported on Wednesday that the operatives convinced a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to appear on the ballot alongside the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola’s campaign asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s updated lawsuit. "Nothing in these new allegations changes DOJ’s utter lack of any legal claim, any legal authority to bring this case, or any entitlement to the relief it seeks," Peltola’s lawyers wrote in their motion. Her campaign has previously said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races. Daniel J. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as unaffiliated with any party, has previously denied that his aim was to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan. Julie Wyatt, a 62-year-old logistics manager who lives in the capital Juneau, said such trickery was nothing new in Alaskan politics, and she still planned to vote for Peltola. "If the Republicans are this desperate, Mary has them on the ropes," she wrote in an email. CALIFORNIA SUBPOENAS In California, meanwhile, the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week in the Justice Department’s investigation into alleged non-citizen voting. "At every step, the US Department ​of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach," Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement ​on Thursday. "Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law." A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the subpoenas but said that California and the federal government "agree that non-citizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law."

items.excerpt: 'Time is the fire in which we burn': 2 major cast losses rock the passionate 'Star Trek' universe WASHINGTON (AP) — First Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original series during the 1960s, died at age 90. Then, three days later, the cosmos lost Patrick Stewart. The Shakespearean actor in 1987 became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, the unlikely and poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have made the present sting. William Shatner played Capt. James T. Kirk in the original series in the 1960s. He called it a “heartbreaking week.” Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86 Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a “Star Trek” franchise and the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86. A spokesperson said Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia. Stewart was best known as Professor Charles Xavier from the “X-Men” and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” but he spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. ... Music Review: Daddy Yankee's first concept album, 'La Postal,' is a reggaeton love letter New York (AP) — The reggaeton icon Daddy Yankee has released a new album, “La Postal,” marking another chapter in his evolving career. This 15-track concept album, which translates to “The Postcard” in English, is a love letter to various forms of adoration, including romantic, familial and self-love, focusing on themes of affection and unity. Collaborations with newer generation artists like Myke Towers, Bizarrap, and Cardi B highlight his role as a trailblazer in Latin music. The album closes with “Pokito,” a cross-cultural collaboration with Indian American superstar Diljit Dosanjh. Associated Press Music Writer Maria Sherman writes that the single is yet another example of Yankee bringing regional music to the global stage.
